course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: The Global Tapestry
unit.description: Explore how societies organized power, shared beliefs, and built their economies across the world.

framework.name: InSPECT
framework.title: Use InSPECT to choose your evidence
framework.intro: A fact can connect to more than one lens. Choose the lens that helps answer the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Based on the class Early Religions + InSPECT slides, pages 5-17.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Maya political organization?
choices: Rival city-states shared cultural traditions until Mayapan united them into an empire
A single Maya emperor ruled all cities from Tenochtitlan after 1325
Rival city-states shared cultural traditions but had no single permanent government
Maya cities were governed as provinces of the Mexica Triple Alliance
questions.explanation: Maya cities competed and allied with one another while sharing writing, calendars, and religion.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Mayapan was powerful in the later period, but it did not create a lasting empire over all Maya cities.
Tenochtitlan was the Mexica capital, not a Maya one.
Maya cities competed and allied with one another while sharing writing, calendars, and religion.
Most Maya cities lay outside Mexica control.

questions.prompt: Why was retaining local rulers useful to the Mexica tributary system?
choices: Local rulers delivered tribute, while Mexica military power enforced it
Local rulers became Mexica nobles and moved to Tenochtitlan
Local rulers kept tribute for themselves in exchange for loyalty
Local rulers delivered tribute, so the Mexica no longer needed to maintain an army
questions.explanation: Using existing leaders saved the cost of direct rule, while the threat of force kept tribute flowing.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Using existing leaders saved the cost of direct rule, while the threat of force kept tribute flowing.
Most local rulers stayed in their own communities.
Tribute went to the alliance; that was its purpose.
Local delivery is right, but force remained essential to the system.
questions.distinguisher: Indirect rule worked because force backed it.

questions.prompt: What was the main relationship between chinampas and Tenochtitlan’s growth?
choices: Chinampas let the city export most of its maize to the Andes
Intensive farming near the city made tribute from other regions unnecessary
Chinampas protected the city from attack by surrounding it with water
Intensive farming near the city helped feed a large urban population
questions.explanation: Raised beds in the lake produced crops close to the city, supporting its growth.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Mesoamerica and the Andes did not trade maize on such a scale.
Chinampas mattered, but tribute still brought food and goods from elsewhere.
The lake helped defense, but chinampas were mainly agricultural.
Raised beds in the lake produced crops close to the city, supporting its growth.
questions.distinguisher: Chinampas were one food source among several.

questions.prompt: How did mit’a obligations strengthen Inca administration?
choices: They provided rotating labor, which was paid in gold coins by the state
They provided rotating labor for roads, farms, armies, and storehouses
They required every household to move permanently to Cusco
They let communities pay taxes in silver instead of goods or work
questions.explanation: Communities owed periods of work to the state, which built and supplied the empire.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Rotating labor is right, but the Inca did not use coined money.
Communities owed periods of work to the state, which built and supplied the empire.
Mit'a was a rotating obligation, not permanent relocation.
Inca obligations were met mainly through labor, not silver payments.
questions.distinguisher: Labor, not money, was the Inca tax.

questions.prompt: What inference is supported by Inca roads, relay messengers, and khipus?
choices: Merchants used wheeled carts to move goods along the roads
The state coordinated information and supplies across difficult terrain
Each region governed itself without contact with Cusco
The state coordinated information, which was written in alphabetic script
questions.explanation: Roads, runners, and knotted-cord records let officials manage people and resources over long distances.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Andean transport relied on people and llamas, not wheeled carts.
Roads, runners, and knotted-cord records let officials manage people and resources over long distances.
These tools existed precisely to connect regions to the center.
Coordination is right, but khipus were knotted cords, not alphabetic writing.
questions.distinguisher: Infrastructure plus record keeping equals coordination.

questions.prompt: Which comparison accurately connects farming to geography?
choices: Both were techniques for herding llamas in high mountain pastures
Chinampas used Andean slopes, while terraces used lake environments
Both used irrigation canals in flat desert regions of North America
Chinampas used lake environments, while terraces managed Andean slopes
questions.explanation: Each technique answered a different environmental challenge.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Both were farming methods, not herding techniques.
This reverses the two techniques.
Neither describes desert farming in North America.
Each technique answered a different environmental challenge.

questions.prompt: Why is European disease an unsuitable explanation for Mesa Verde’s thirteenth-century relocation?
choices: The relocation happened centuries before Europeans reached the region
The relocation happened before Europeans arrived, so disease played no role anywhere
Ancestral Pueblo people were immune to all diseases
Spanish settlers founded Mesa Verde as a mission town
questions.explanation: Europeans arrived in the Southwest in the 1500s; drought and resource pressures fit the 1200s.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Europeans arrived in the Southwest in the 1500s; drought and resource pressures fit the 1200s.
The timing rules out European disease here, but disease was a real factor in later centuries.
No population was immune to all diseases.
Ancestral Pueblo people built Mesa Verde long before Spanish contact.
questions.distinguisher: Check chronology before accepting a cause.

questions.prompt: What can Cahokia’s large earthen mounds most directly support?
choices: The city's residents were all of roughly equal social rank and wealth
The mounds were built by migrants from Mesoamerica
The community organized large amounts of labor and resources
The community organized labor under a written law code
questions.explanation: Building massive mounds required coordinating many workers and food supplies.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Burials and buildings suggest social ranking, not equality.
Cahokia was built by Mississippian peoples of the region.
Building massive mounds required coordinating many workers and food supplies.
Mounds show organized labor, but Cahokia left no written records.
questions.distinguisher: Claim only what the evidence can show.

choices: A record kept on knotted cords by state officials
Goods traded voluntarily between merchants at a market
A gift that rulers gave to their subjects at festivals
Goods or labor that a subject community is required to provide
questions.explanation: Tribute was a required payment imposed on conquered or subordinate communities.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: That describes a khipu.
Market exchange was voluntary; tribute was required.
Tribute flowed to rulers, not from them.
Tribute was a required payment imposed on conquered or subordinate communities.

questions.prompt: Which tool helped Inca officials keep records?
choices: Chinampas in the lake
Codices painted on bark
Khipus of knotted cords
Stelae carved in stone
questions.explanation: Khipus recorded numbers and other information with knots.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Chinampas were Mexica farming plots.
Painted codices are associated with Mesoamerica.
Khipus recorded numbers and other information with knots.
Carved stelae are associated with the Maya.

questions.prompt: What continued after the decline of many Classic Maya centers?
choices: A single permanent empire uniting all of the Maya cities
Maya communities, languages, and later centers such as Mayapan
Mexica imperial control over the entire Yucatán Peninsula
Maya rule over the distant Inca, who paid them regular tribute
questions.explanation: Maya peoples and cities continued, and Maya languages are spoken today.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.4 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: No single empire united all Maya cities.
Maya peoples and cities continued, and Maya languages are spoken today.
The Mexica did not control the Yucatán.
The Maya never ruled the Inca.
questions.distinguisher: A city's decline is not the end of a people.
